chunks: Ali, from his father, from Ibn Mahboub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Zurara, who said:

My mother had made a vow upon herself; she vowed to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, regarding one of her children, concerning something she feared for him, that she would fast the day that came upon her for as long as she lived. So she traveled with us to Mecca, and it became confusing for us regarding her fasting during the journey, so she did not know whether to fast or break her fast. So I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about that, and he said: 'She should not fast during the journey, for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has removed His right from her during the journey, and she should fast what she made upon herself.' So I said to him, 'So what is that when she returns, if she leaves that (fasting)?' He said: 'No, I fear that she will see in her child, regarding whom she vowed, some of what she dislikes.'
ai.seo_question: How does a traveler fulfill a vow to fast if they are unsure whether to fast or break fast during the journey?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the Shia juristic principle that travel exemptions (rukhas) apply to the obligatory aspect of a vow, allowing the vow-maker to break the fast during travel without penalty. Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) further clarifies that the vow is not extinguished by the travel exemption; rather, the obligation to fast resumes upon her return to ensure the specific condition of her vow is fully met. This ruling highlights the distinction between the temporary suspension of duty due to hardship and the permanent fulfillment of the vowed commitment.
